advances: Proves a dimension-uniform reflected-mass bound for every nonnegative exponential tilt on an arbitrary positive-coefficient integer knapsack, including irrational coefficients, zero tilt, zero resource, and simultaneous discrete-center jumps. The elementary scalar theorem has the explicit absolute constant e^-50 and uses no accepted dependency. Composing it with accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14` also proves the weak Oertel depth bound for convex bodies whose positive integer-fiber support is such a knapsack and whose fiber volumes are within a fixed multiplicative factor of a scaled exponential profile. No assertion is made that arbitrary convex bodies satisfy this additional profile hypothesis.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The scalar argument is elementary. The convex-body consequence uses only the declared accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`, with its actual fiber-volume objects and its cutoff depth conclusion as specified in the proof.
proof:
The set \(A\) is finite because \(0\le z_i\le R/b_i\) for \(z\in A\), and it contains zero. In particular, \(\widetilde W>0\). We first prove the scalar assertion without using the accepted predecessor.

For \(q\in(0,1)\), consider \((2m+1)q^m\) on integers \(m\ge0\). Its successive ratio is \(q(2m+3)/(2m+1)\), strictly decreasing in \(m\), and the sequence tends to zero. Put \(t_m:=(2m-1)/(2m+1)\) for \(m\ge1\). The integer zero maximizes the sequence exactly when \(q\le1/3\); an integer \(m\ge1\) maximizes it exactly when \(t_m\le q\le t_{m+1}\). At \(q=t_m\), the only maximizers are \(m-1,m\). At every other value of \(q\), there is a unique maximizer.

For every integer \(m\ge1\),

\[
m\log\frac{2m+1}{2m-1}
=\int_0^{1/2}\frac{2}{1-(s/m)^2}\,ds
\le\int_0^{1/2}\frac{2}{1-s^2}\,ds
=\log3.
\]

Consequently \(t_m^m\ge1/3\). For \(m\ge1\), the logarithm of \(2(1-q)(2m+1)q^m\) is concave on \([t_m,t_{m+1}]\), so its minimum on that interval is attained at an endpoint. The endpoint values are \(4t_m^m\) and \(4t_{m+1}^{m+1}\), each at least \(4/3\). For \(m=0\) and \(q\le1/3\), the value is \(2(1-q)\ge4/3\). Moreover, if a maximizing integer \(m\) is positive, then \(q\ge t_m\) and \(m(-\log q)\le\log3\le2\). Thus every maximizing integer satisfies

\[
2(1-q)(2m+1)q^m\ge\frac43,
\qquad m(-\log q)\le2\quad\text{if }m\ge1.
\tag{1}
\]

For \(j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n\), define \(\sigma_a(j)^2:=\sum_i a_i^2j_i(j_i+1)/3\), \(\sigma_b(j)^2:=\sum_i b_i^2j_i(j_i+1)/3\), and \(F(j):=b\cdot j+2\sigma_b(j)\). These are nonnegative, and \(F\) is nondecreasing in each coordinate. We next construct a finite \(\lambda\ge0\) and a vector \(j\) such that every \(j_i\) maximizes \((2m+1)q_i(\lambda)^m\), where \(q_i(\lambda):=e^{-(a_i+\lambda b_i)}\in(0,1)\), and

\[
F(j)\le R,
\qquad
\lambda(R-b\cdot j)\le2\lambda\sigma_b(j)+6.
\tag{2}
\]

For any \(\lambda\) for which all \(q_i(\lambda)<1\), let \(m_i(\lambda)\) be the smallest maximizing integer. Each \(m_i(\lambda)\) is nonincreasing in \(\lambda\). Its jumps occur when \(q_i(\lambda)=t_k\), and each jump decreases the coordinate from \(k\) to \(k-1\). At the jump value both integers maximize the sequence, and the smallest-maximizer convention selects the latter.

If every \(a_i>0\) and \(F(m(0))\le R\), choose \(\lambda=0\), \(j=m(0)\); then (2) holds. In every other case there is a \(\delta>0\) with \(F(m(\delta))>R\). Indeed, if every \(a_i>0\) and \(F(m(0))>R\), the smallest-maximizer convention makes each coordinate constant immediately to the right of zero, so any sufficiently small positive \(\delta\) works. If some \(a_i=0\), then \(q_i(\lambda)\) tends to one as \(\lambda\) decreases to zero, and the characterization \(q_i(\lambda)\le t_{m_i(\lambda)+1}\) forces \(m_i(\lambda)\) to tend to infinity. Since \(b_i>0\), this again gives \(F(m(\delta))>R\) for sufficiently small positive \(\delta\).

Choose a finite \(\lambda_+>\delta\) such that \(q_i(\lambda_+)<1/3\) for every \(i\). Then \(m(\lambda_+)=0\), so \(F(m(\lambda_+))=0\le R\). There are only finitely many jump events on \((\delta,\lambda_+]\): every coordinate starts at the finite nonnegative integer \(m_i(\delta)\), never increases, and loses exactly one at each of its subsequent events. Order these events by their real values of \(\lambda\). At an event with several tied coordinates, perform the tied decrements one at a time in any order. Every intermediate vector still consists entirely of maximizers at that same value of \(\lambda\). This construction is independent of whether the numbers \(b_i\) are rational.

Since \(F\) starts above \(R\) and ends at zero, there is a first decrement that changes \(F\) from a value above \(R\) to one at most \(R\). Let its parameter be \(\lambda\), its resulting vector be \(j\), and its previous vector be \(\widehat j=j+e_i\). Set \(k:=\widehat j_i=j_i+1\ge1\). Then \(q_i(\lambda)=t_k\), and (1), applied to the maximizing integer \(k\), gives \(\lambda b_i\le a_i+\lambda b_i=-\log t_k\le2/k\). Also

\[
\sigma_b(\widehat j)^2-\sigma_b(j)^2
=\frac{2b_i^2k}{3},
\qquad
F(\widehat j)-F(j)
\le b_i\left(1+2\sqrt{\frac{2k}{3}}\right).
\]

The second inequality uses \(\sqrt{x+y}-\sqrt x\le\sqrt y\) for \(x,y\ge0\). Because \(F(j)\le R<F(\widehat j)\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda(R-F(j))
&<\lambda b_i\left(1+2\sqrt{\frac{2k}{3}}\right)\\
&\le\frac2k+4\sqrt{\frac{2}{3k}}
\le2+4\sqrt{\frac23}<6.
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding \(2\lambda\sigma_b(j)\) proves (2). This completes the construction, including \(R=0\) and simultaneous ties. In particular, \(j\in A\), all \(q_i(\lambda)<1\), and each \(j_i\) is maximizing at the chosen \(\lambda\).

Fix this choice and write \(\sigma_a:=\sigma_a(j)\), \(\sigma_b:=\sigma_b(j)\), \(q_i:=q_i(\lambda)\). If \(j_i\ge1\), (1) gives \((a_i+\lambda b_i)j_i\le2\). Nonnegativity of \(a_i,\lambda b_i\) therefore implies \(a_i j_i\le2\) and \(\lambda b_i j_i\le2\). Each corresponding term in \(\sigma_a^2\) or \(\lambda^2\sigma_b^2\) is at most \(4(j_i+1)/(3j_i)\le8/3\), and coordinates with \(j_i=0\) contribute zero. Hence

\[
\sigma_a^2\le\frac{8n}{3},
\qquad
\lambda^2\sigma_b^2\le\frac{8n}{3}.
\tag{3}
\]

Let the random variables \(V_i\) be independent and uniform on \(\{-j_i,\ldots,j_i\}\). They have mean zero and variance \(j_i(j_i+1)/3\), so \(a\cdot V\) and \(b\cdot V\) have variances \(\sigma_a^2\) and \(\sigma_b^2\). Chebyshev's inequality and a union bound give
\(\mathbb P\{|a\cdot V|\le2\sigma_a,\ |b\cdot V|\le2\sigma_b\}\ge1/2\).
If either variance is zero, its random variable is identically zero, so the same assertion holds without dividing by that variance.

On this event, both \(j+V\) and \(j-V\) have nonnegative integer coordinates, and \(b\cdot(j\pm V)\le b\cdot j+2\sigma_b\le R\). Thus both endpoints belong to \(A\). On the same event their minimum weight equals \(e^{-a\cdot j-|a\cdot V|}\), which is at least \(e^{-a\cdot j-2\sigma_a}\). Since the distribution of \(V\) is uniform on a box of cardinality \(\prod_i(2j_i+1)\),

\[
\widetilde S_j
\ge\frac12e^{-a\cdot j-2\sigma_a}\prod_i(2j_i+1).
\tag{4}
\]

For \(z\in A\), the exponential tilt gives \(e^{-a\cdot z}=e^{\lambda b\cdot z}\prod_iq_i^{z_i}\le e^{\lambda R}\prod_iq_i^{z_i}\). Since \(0<q_i<1\), summing and then extending the sum to the whole nonnegative integer orthant yields \(\widetilde W\le e^{\lambda R}\prod_i(1-q_i)^{-1}\). Combining this with (4), (1), (2), and (3), respectively, gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\widetilde S_j}{2^{-n}\widetilde W}
&\ge\frac12e^{-2\sigma_a-\lambda(R-b\cdot j)}
\prod_i\bigl[2(1-q_i)(2j_i+1)q_i^{j_i}\bigr]\\
&\ge\frac12\exp\left(n\log\frac43-2\sigma_a-\lambda(R-b\cdot j)\right)\\
&\ge\frac12\exp\left(n\log\frac43-4\sqrt{\frac{8n}{3}}-6\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]

Finally, \(\log(4/3)=\int_1^{4/3}t^{-1}\,dt\ge1/4\), and completing the square gives

\[
\frac n4-4\sqrt{\frac{8n}{3}}
=\left(\frac{\sqrt n}{2}-4\sqrt{\frac83}\right)^2-\frac{128}{3}
\ge-\frac{128}{3}.
\]

Using also \(\log2\le1\), the logarithm of the last expression in (5) is at least \(-1-6-128/3=-149/3>-50\). This proves \(\widetilde S_j\ge e^{-50}2^{-n}\widetilde W\).

We now prove the convex-body consequence. Here the objects \(C_z,w_z,W,S,h_S\) have exactly their meanings in accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`; the scalar weights \(\widetilde w_z\) used above are not substituted for actual fiber volumes. For the center \(j\in A\) obtained above, define \(\alpha(v):=\min\{w_{j+v},w_{j-v}\}\), \(\mathcal U_j:=\{v:\alpha(v)>0\}\), and \(\Delta_j(v):=\log(w_j^2/(w_{j+v}w_{j-v}))\) for \(v\in\mathcal U_j\), exactly as in that predecessor. It gives \(\Delta_j(v)\ge0\). The support hypothesis ensures that all actual and model weights vanish outside \(A\). The assumed comparison therefore gives, for every integer displacement \(v\),
\(\alpha(v)\ge(K/M)\min\{\widetilde w_{j+v},\widetilde w_{j-v}\}\), and it gives \(W\le KM\widetilde W\). Consequently

\[
\sum_v\alpha(v)
\ge\frac K M\widetilde S_j
\ge\frac{K e^{-50}}M\,2^{-n}\widetilde W
\ge\frac{e^{-50}}{M^2}\,2^{-n}W.
\tag{6}
\]

For \(v\in\mathcal U_j\), both endpoints belong to \(A\), and the same comparison explicitly bounds the curvature:

\[
\frac{w_j^2}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}
\le
\frac{(KM e^{-a\cdot j})^2}
{(KM^{-1}e^{-a\cdot(j+v)})(KM^{-1}e^{-a\cdot(j-v)})}
=M^4.
\]

Thus \(0\le\Delta_j(v)\le4\log M\) for every positive pair. With \(L:=4\log M\ge0\), the predecessor's cutoff sum \(B_j^\Delta(L):=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j:\Delta_j(v)\le L}\alpha(v)\) equals \(\sum_v\alpha(v)\). Apply the cutoff conclusion of accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14` to this actual convex body. Its hypotheses hold because \(n,d\ge1\), \(C\) is a convex body, and \(w_0\ge K/M>0\), so \(W>0\). Its maximum over centers and cutoffs is at least this chosen value of \(B_j^\Delta(L)/(1+L)\). It supplies one point \(p^\star\in S\) for which

\[
h_S(p^\star)
\ge\frac{\ell}{16}\frac{B_j^\Delta(4\log M)}{1+4\log M}
\ge\frac{\ell e^{-50}}{16M^2(1+4\log M)}\,2^{-n}W,
\]

where the last inequality is (6). The accepted conclusion selects this point before the ambient halfspace, so the bound has the required simultaneous halfspace quantifier. The scale \(K\) has canceled. This proves the stated corollary under its explicit support and profile hypotheses.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer, let \(a_i\ge0\), \(b_i>0\) for \(1\le i\le n\), and let \(R\ge0\). Define \(A:=\{z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n:b\cdot z\le R\}\). For every \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), let \(\widetilde w_z:=e^{-a\cdot z}\) if \(z\in A\), and let \(\widetilde w_z:=0\) otherwise. Put \(\widetilde W:=\sum_z\widetilde w_z\) and \(\widetilde S_j:=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}\min\{\widetilde w_{j+v},\widetilde w_{j-v}\}\). Then there exists \(j\in A\) such that \(\widetilde S_j\ge e^{-50}2^{-n}\widetilde W\).

There is also the following consequence for actual convex bodies. Let \(d\ge1\), let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, put \(C_z:=\{x:(z,x)\in C\}\), and let \(w_z:=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z)\). Assume that its positive-volume integer-fiber support is exactly \(A\). Suppose that there are numbers \(K>0\), \(M\ge1\) such that \(KM^{-1}e^{-a\cdot z}\le w_z\le KM e^{-a\cdot z}\) for every \(z\in A\). Put \(W:=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}w_z\), \(S:=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\), and let \(h_S(p)\) be the infimum of \(\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\) over closed ambient halfspaces containing \(p\), exactly as in the locked problem and accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`. With \(\ell:=-\log(1-e^{-1})\), there exists one point \(p^\star\in S\) satisfying

\[
h_S(p^\star)\ge
\frac{\ell e^{-50}}{16M^2(1+4\log M)}\,2^{-n}W.
\]

For each fixed \(M\), this positive constant is independent of \(n,d,a,b,R,K\). The tilded quantities are the auxiliary scalar profile; the untilded fiber volumes and mixed-volume quantities have precisely their meanings in the accepted predecessor. All logarithms are natural.
